title: Octet in E-flat major
hook: Eight string players and a sixteen-year-old composer at full speed.

painting.title: The Friedrichsgracht, Berlin
painting.pairingNote: Rooftops and a canal in the heart of Berlin under a bright sky, painted by a Berlin artist in the decade after the Octet, which the sixteen-year-old Mendelssohn wrote in the same city.
painting.medium: Oil on paper, mounted on paper-fibre based board

facts: Mendelssohn wrote the Octet in Berlin in the autumn of 1825 and finished it on 15 October. He was sixteen. He gave the score to his friend and violin teacher Eduard Rietz as a birthday present.

It is written for four violins, two violas and two cellos. In Louis Spohr’s double quartets, two separate quartets face each other; Mendelssohn treats the eight as one ensemble, and wrote in the score that it must be played “in symphonic orchestral style”, with louds and softs sharper than usual.

The scherzo is thought to have been inspired by the “Walpurgis Night’s Dream” in Goethe’s *Faust*, a scene of spirits and fairies that ends with mist lifting and everything vanishing. Mendelssohn later orchestrated this movement and used it in place of the minuet of his First Symphony.
Music from the scherzo comes back in the finale, and the finale opens with all eight players entering one after another. The work was revised before it was published in 1832.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a soaring, symphonic opening (I), a lilting song in the minor (II), a whispered flight of spirits (III), a race in which all eight voices chase each other (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro moderato ma con fuoco
movements.summary: The first violin climbs in great leaps over a shimmering, throbbing accompaniment from the other seven, and the music sounds less like chamber music than like a small orchestra. The movement is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]] and takes almost half the length of the work.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, first violin
mainIdeas.description: a rising tune that leaps upwards in long strides, over quick, trembling chords.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a quieter, gentler melody, moving in smaller steps, shared among the upper instruments.

stops.hear: The first violin soars upwards in wide leaps; underneath, the other players shiver with quick repeated notes
stops.happening: Theme 1, in E-flat major, over a [[tremolo|tremolo]]-like accompaniment

stops.hear: The tune moves down into the cellos and violas while the violins rush above
stops.happening: The theme passes to the lower instruments

stops.hear: Calmer and sweeter: a gentle melody in smaller steps
Busy, bright figures in all eight parts and a strong close
The soaring opening tune starts again
Pieces of Theme 1 move into darker keys and pass from player to player
Very quiet, long-held notes; then the movement starts to rise, faster and louder, until all eight are racing
stops.happening: The long build at the end of the development

stops.hear: The first violin’s leaping tune returns in full
The music gathers speed and energy

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Loud, emphatic chords from all eight players

notice: In the first minute, listen under the violin’s tune. Seven players keep up a quick, trembling pulse, and that pulse is what makes the music sound orchestral.
In the build-up at the end of the development, notice how the music starts from almost nothing: long, quiet notes that gradually break into quicker and quicker motion.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The players are members of the Academy of St Martin in the Fields, among them Neville Marriner and Iona Brown, recorded at Kingsway Hall, London, in 1967. They play the repeat of the exposition, which is why the first movement lasts over fourteen minutes. On the Spotify album the Octet is tracks 1–4, followed by a cello quintet by Boccherini.

movements.heading: Andante
movements.summary: A slow movement in C minor with a gentle, rocking lilt, like a song in a swaying rhythm. The eight voices move closely together, sometimes in rich chords, sometimes in simple lines; the mood is tender rather than tragic.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a lilting melody in six, first heard low in the ensemble and then rising to the violins.

mainIdeas.name: The answer
mainIdeas.description: a warmer passage in a major key, with the parts weaving around each other.

stops.hear: A quiet, rocking melody in the lower and middle voices
stops.happening: The opening song, in C minor

stops.hear: The violins take the melody higher; the harmony becomes richer
stops.happening: The theme rises through the ensemble

stops.hear: A warmer, more flowing passage in a major key
The music darkens and wanders through more distant keys; the lines tangle and press forward
stops.happening: The middle of the movement, where the ideas are worked

stops.hear: The rocking opening returns

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The voices thin out and the movement closes very softly in C minor

notice: Listen to how often the eight players move together in one rhythm, almost like a choir, before splitting into separate lines.

movements.heading: Scherzo: Allegro leggierissimo
movements.summary: Very fast and very quiet: tiny, detached notes flicker from one player to another, never settling. Mendelssohn’s marking means “as light as possible”. It was probably inspired by Goethe’s spirits, and it ends as if everything had simply blown away.

mainIdeas.name: The flicker
mainIdeas.description: quick, short, whispered notes in G minor, passed between the instruments.

mainIdeas.name: The flights
mainIdeas.description: little runs and trills that dart upwards in the violins.

stops.hear: Whispered, quick, detached notes, passed from one player to another
stops.happening: The [[scherzo|scherzo]] theme, in G minor. Almost everything here is played very softly

stops.hear: A brighter tune in a major key, still light and quick
Fragments chase each other through all eight parts
stops.happening: The middle of the movement, where the ideas are worked

stops.hear: The whispered opening returns

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The music grows thinner and quieter, and vanishes upwards
stops.happening: The ending: “and everything has vanished”, as in Goethe’s scene

notice: Try to hear how soft this movement is. Eight string players almost never play loudly here, and the effect depends on that restraint.

movements.heading: Presto
movements.summary: The finale starts in the depths: the second cello alone sets off with a rushing tune, and the others enter one after another, upwards, until all eight are racing. Later the whispering music of the scherzo slips back in. It is a [[fugato|fugato]] that turns into a high-speed celebration.

mainIdeas.name: The race
mainIdeas.description: a quick, rushing tune that each instrument takes up in turn.

mainIdeas.name: The quotation
mainIdeas.description: a broad, hymn-like phrase that recalls “And he shall reign for ever and ever” from the “Hallelujah” Chorus in Handel’s *Messiah*.

mainIdeas.name: The return
mainIdeas.description: the scherzo’s flickering theme, heard again inside the finale.

stops.hear: The second cello alone rushes off with a quick, rumbling tune; one by one the others join, each higher than the last
stops.happening: An eight-part [[fugato|fugato]], from the lowest instrument to the highest

stops.hear: All eight together, loud; a short, punching figure in octaves
A broad phrase rings out above the rushing notes
stops.happening: Mendelssohn quotes Handel’s “And he shall reign for ever and ever”

stops.hear: Suddenly lighter: the scherzo’s whispering theme returns, now in the finale’s speed
stops.happening: Music from the third movement comes back, an early example of [[cyclic-form|cyclic form]]

stops.hear: The rushing tune enters again in voice after voice

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: All eight players drive to a loud, emphatic end

notice: In the first seconds, count the entries from the bottom upwards: cello, cello, violas, violins. By the time the first violin enters, all eight are playing.
When the scherzo’s theme returns, listen for how quickly it is swept back into the race.

threads.title: A small orchestra
threads.body: Mendelssohn asked for a symphonic style, and the Octet often sounds bigger than eight players: trembling accompaniments, sharp contrasts of loud and soft, all the voices together.

threads.title: Spirits
threads.body: The scherzo’s lightness, linked with Goethe’s *Faust*, returns in the finale. The next year Mendelssohn wrote the overture to *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*, with the same fairy lightness.

threads.title: Counterpoint
threads.body: From the finale’s fugato to the voices chasing each other in the scherzo, the sixteen-year-old shows off his [[counterpoint|counterpoint]].
